solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: I'm disgusted about Left's claptrap

indicators.note: 'about' means around, so one piece is wrapped round another

parts.note: L is the standard abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Someone recoils from the nonsense spouted by the political Left.
explanation.walkthrough: BAH goes round L; the 's after Left is just the possessive of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe empty, pretentious talk that means nothing at all, so they are straightforward synonyms.

clue.text: Flexible untruths told by chap with lisp

indicators.note: something told is spoken, and a lisper turns every S sound into a TH sound

parts.note: untruths are lies; with a lisp the final Z sound becomes TH

explanation.surface: A man with a lisp tells convenient, bendable fibs.
explanation.walkthrough: Say LIES with a lisp and the Z becomes a TH, giving exactly the sound of LITHE.
explanation.definitionFit: A lithe body is supple and bends easily, which is what being flexible means physically.

clue.text: Why is that old toilet in Habitat?

indicators.note: 'in' places one thing inside another, so the first pieces sit within the last

parts.note: O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Someone asks why an antique lavatory is on sale in Habitat, the British furniture and homeware store.
explanation.walkthrough: Habitat, capitalised to look like the shop name, is just a home; O and WC go inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: The colloquial question is used to ask for the reason behind something, exactly like asking for an explanation.

clue.text: Senate group renowned for giving a hoot

definitions.text: group renowned for giving a hoot
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the collective noun for owls, birds famous for hooting

explanation.surface: A senate committee is praised for actually caring about things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Giving a hoot' looks like the idiom for caring, but it is literal: owls hoot, and a group of owls has a special collective name.
explanation.definitionFit: A senate is a lawmaking assembly, and the same word is the traditional collective noun for a flock of owls.

clue.text: Go on a brief river excursion at the front

indicators.note: something brief is cut short, so the final letter is lost

parts.note: 'a' as in 'per', e.g. five pounds a head

indicators.note: the front of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

explanation.surface: An invitation to take a short boat trip upriver, sitting at the front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A' meaning PER is a common crossword equivalence (so much a day = so much per day). SEVERN loses its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To go on in the face of difficulty is to keep going steadily, which is the sense of the verb.

clue.text: No rubbish dumping close to a lake

indicators.note: the close of a word is its last letter, and dumping it means throwing it away

parts.note: L is the standard abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A sign forbidding fly-tipping beside a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No rubbish dumping' reads as a notice; in fact 'No' is the definition and 'dumping close' strips the end from REFUSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying no to a request is turning it down, and that act is a refusal (noun used as a negative answer).

clue.text: United foolish to sub centre for Oscar

indicators.note: to sub is to substitute, swapping the middle letter for a new one

parts.note: Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A football manager at United is mocked for bringing on a substitute called Oscar in the centre.
explanation.walkthrough: The middle A of INANE is replaced by O.
explanation.definitionFit: Things joined in one are combined into a single whole, the sense of being united together.

clue.text: Moderate cold? Drug will get rid of that!

indicators.note: getting rid of something removes it, here the letter just mentioned

parts.note: to drug someone is to medicate them
C is the standard abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: An advert promising that a drug will cure a mild cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moderate cold' reads as a mild illness, but Moderate is the verb defining the answer; 'that' points back to cold, the C removed from MEDICATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To moderate a dispute is to act as go-between and bring the sides together, a synonym for this verb.

clue.text: Nobody else at work up here, not surprisingly

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: a machine that is working is on

indicators.note: a surprising outcome is unexpected, so the letters come out in an unexpected order

explanation.surface: An office worker notes that, unsurprisingly, nobody else has come in to work upstairs.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'up' reads the piece bottom to top; 'not surprisingly' looks like an aside but is the anagram signal for the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase as in 'none other than' means no different person, so it equates to nobody else.

clue.text: Do not wed fool or knight or Old Nick

indicators.note: to do something up is to fix or rework it, so the letters are made over

parts.note: N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: Marriage advice: don't marry a fool, a knight, or the Devil himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do not' reads as a command, but Do is the anagram signal. Old Nick is a name for the Devil, yet nick is British slang for prison, so 'old nick' is an old prison.
explanation.definitionFit: The historic London fortress long served as a state prison, so it is a cryptic example of an ancient jail.

clue.text: Analyse and understand river-dwelling fish

indicators.note: something dwelling somewhere lives inside it, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: the Dee, a river in Britain

explanation.surface: A biologist studies freshwater fish to understand them.
explanation.walkthrough: The fish is placed inside the river, rather than the river being a description of the fish.
explanation.definitionFit: To decode a message is to work through it and grasp its meaning, which covers both analysing and understanding.

clue.text: Furniture maker that girl found by shop

parts.note: to shop someone is British slang for informing on them

explanation.surface: A girl discovers a cabinet-maker by visiting his shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Shop is a verb here: to shop someone to the police is to rat on them.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Sheraton was an eighteenth-century English cabinet designer whose name became a style of furniture.

clue.text: Take care of diet in a satisfactory way

definitions.note: a parting phrase, answering a noun or interjection of goodbye

explanation.surface: Advice to watch what you eat so you eat properly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take care of diet' reads as health advice; 'Take care' is actually the goodbye, with 'of' as a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Take care is said when parting from someone, so it serves as a goodbye or valediction.

clue.text: Drama set rebuilt with millions in capital

indicators.note: something rebuilt is put together again in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: M is the standard abbreviation for million

explanation.surface: A theatre set is reconstructed at a cost of millions in a capital city.
explanation.walkthrough: The M joins the anagram letters before they are shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Amsterdam is the official capital city of the Netherlands, so it is an example of a capital.

clue.text: Brownie brought over by shrink makes you fat

indicators.note: bringing something over flips it, turning it back to front

parts.note: a brownie is a household sprite, a kind of elf
to shrink or shy away from something

explanation.surface: A chocolate brownie handed over by your psychiatrist will put on weight.
explanation.walkthrough: Brownie is the folklore sprite, not the cake, and shrink is the verb, not slang for a psychiatrist.
explanation.definitionFit: Fleshy and fat both describe a plump body carrying plenty of soft tissue, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Troublemaker in bar friend sorted out

indicators.note: sorting things out puts them into a new order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A pub friend deals with a rowdy drinker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is only a link; the fodder is just 'bar friend'.
explanation.definitionFit: A firebrand stirs up conflict and agitation, which makes such a person a classic troublemaker or agitator.

clue.text: Grounds, say, to go after head of Exxon

indicators.note: going after means following, so one piece is placed behind the other
the head of a word is its opening letter

explanation.surface: Someone has reasons to pursue the boss of the oil company Exxon.
explanation.walkthrough: Grounds looks like reasons, but it means land.
explanation.definitionFit: The grounds of a country house are its surrounding land, which is what an estate is.

clue.text: A small problem with Queen impersonator?

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small

explanation.surface: A minor difficulty with someone who impersonates the Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: ER, for Elizabeth Regina, is the usual crossword Queen.
explanation.definitionFit: One who assumes another's identity or role takes it on falsely, which is what an impersonator does.

clue.text: Geek abruptly, after blocking pieces, mates

indicators.note: blocking a path means standing in the middle of it, so one piece sits inside another
something ending abruptly is cut off before its end, losing the last letter

explanation.surface: A chess geek suddenly checkmates after hemming in the pieces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mates' suggests checkmate on the chessboard, but it is the plain noun for companions.
explanation.definitionFit: Mates are friends or companions, and partners are people paired together, so the two nouns are synonyms.

clue.text: Meter maid splitting up wordplay for "moralist"

indicators.note: splitting something up drives a wedge into its middle, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: Lovely Rita is the meter maid of the Beatles song

explanation.surface: A traffic warden interrupts some punning to substitute a sterner word.
explanation.walkthrough: Rita is the meter maid (traffic warden) in the Beatles' 'Lovely Rita'.
explanation.definitionFit: A puritan holds strict views on behaviour and disapproves of pleasure, the archetype of a moralist.

clue.text: Love is a matter lacking any importance

definitions.meaning: first meaning: zero, as in a tennis score
second meaning: a trifle, as in 'it's a mere ...'

explanation.surface: A cynic declares that love is trivial.
explanation.walkthrough: Love is the tennis score of zero; the second part is the noun used for something trivial.
explanation.definitionFit: Love in tennis means a score of zero, and the same word names a trifle of no significance.

clue.text: Communication by Queen in Melody Maker

explanation.surface: An interview with the rock band Queen printed in Melody Maker, the British music weekly.
explanation.walkthrough: Melody Maker looks like the magazine, but it means a composer: André Messager was a French composer of operettas.
explanation.definitionFit: A composer creates tunes, so a maker of melodies describes the French operetta writer cryptically.

clue.text: Cottage hospital unit tucked into eggs regularly

indicators.note: tucking something into a thing places it inside
doing something regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the ear, nose and throat department

explanation.surface: A patient in a small country hospital eats eggs regularly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cottage hospital' is a real phrase for a small rural hospital, but Cottage stands alone: in British slang a cottage is a public lavatory.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang uses cottage for a public toilet, and the gents is the men's public toilet.

clue.text: Fight Club line used in film retrospective

indicators.note: retrospective means looking back, so the letters run backwards
something used in a thing is placed inside it

parts.note: L is the standard abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A quotation from the film Fight Club appears in a retrospective of the movie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fight Club' is split: Fight is the definition and Club starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A battle is a fight between opposing forces, so the noun is a direct synonym.

clue.text: Bars in which people usually serve Coke

definitions.text: in which people usually serve Coke
definitions.meaning: second meaning: cocaine is laid out in narrow strips to be snorted

explanation.surface: Pubs where staff tend to pour Coca-Cola.
explanation.walkthrough: Coke is the drug, not the drink, and Bars are strips, not pubs.
explanation.definitionFit: Bars are long narrow stripes, and the same word names the narrow strips in which cocaine is set out.

clue.text: Station having trouble with modern display

indicators.note: something in trouble is in disorder, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A railway station struggles with its new electronic departures board.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words go into the anagram together.
explanation.definitionFit: A demonstration shows how something works, a public showing that counts as a display.

clue.text: Banged-up Mini dopes launched across river

indicators.note: lying across something spans it, so one piece goes round another
something launched is sent flying, scattering the letters into a new order

parts.note: R is the standard abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: Idiots in a dented Mini car drive it into a river.
explanation.walkthrough: Banged-up looks like a dented car, but it is British slang for jailed; the rearranged letters surround R.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang to be banged up is to be locked in prison, so it means jailed.

clue.text: Large cut in fuel hopefully just the start

indicators.note: only the start of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone hopes a big reduction in fuel prices is only the beginning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Large cut' reads as a price reduction, but it is a wound.
explanation.definitionFit: A gash is a long, deep wound in the skin, so it is a big cut.
